content: 1. International and non-governmental organizations are involved in the implementation of health services, which can be either facility-based (such as hospitals, health clinics, and general practice offices) or community-based (such as drop-in centers, community service delivery points, mobile clinics or vans, outreach teams, and community support groups). 2. Cities and other administrative regions of epidemiological importance are identified for targeted interventions and monitoring. 3. Global reporting platforms include the Global AIDS Monitoring system, the WHO Global Hepatitis Reporting System, and tools for validating hepatitis C elimination and progress toward elimination. 4. The proportion of healthcare facilities with safe injection practices is a key indicator for monitoring and evaluation. This includes the use of single-use, standard disposable, or auto-disable syringes to ensure injection safety. 5. The rationale for this indicator is to assess the implementation of policies that ensure all healthcare facilities adhere to safe injection practices. The WHO and the Safe Injection Global Network Alliance have developed tools to evaluate injection safety, including procedures for phlebotomy, lancet use, intravenous injections, and infusions. 6. The Harmonized Health Facility Assessment questionnaire includes questions to evaluate the availability of consumables for standard precautions in infection prevention, such as disposable syringes with disposable needles and auto-disable syringes. 7. The global target is to achieve 100% safe healthcare injections. 8. The numerator for this indicator is the number of sampled healthcare facilities where all therapeutic injections are administered using single-use, standard disposable, or auto-disable syringes. The denominator is the total number of facilities assessed. 9. Measurement methods include health facility surveys, which assess the availability of resources and supplies for infection control in specific service delivery areas such as immunization, emergency departments, obstetric services, surgical services, laboratory services, and outpatient and inpatient services. 10. An alternative approach is to use population surveys, such as Demographic and Health Surveys, to estimate the proportion of injections given from a new, unopened package based on individual data. These estimates are often comparable to data from health facility surveys. 11. Disaggregation of data is performed at national and subnational levels, including facility type (tertiary, secondary, primary) and managing authority (public or private). 12. Global reporting platforms for this indicator include the Harmonized Health Facility Assessment, National Demographic Health Surveys, and the Revised Injection Safety Assessment Tool. 13. The proportion of blood units screened for bloodborne diseases, including hepatitis B and C, is another critical indicator. This measures the implementation of policies to ensure all blood units are screened using quality-assured procedures. 14. The global target for this indicator is 100% screening of blood units for bloodborne diseases. 15. The numerator is the number of blood units screened for bloodborne diseases, including hepatitis B and C, while the denominator is the total number of blood units donated in the reporting year. 16. Data sources for this indicator include program records, the Harmonized Health Facility Assessment, and national demographic health surveys. 17. The proportion of people with chronic hepatitis B who have been diagnosed is a key indicator for testing and diagnosis. It measures the proportion of individuals with chronic hepatitis B (HBsAg positive) who are aware of their infection status. 18. The rationale for this indicator is to estimate the entry point to the continuum of care for people with chronic hepatitis B. Disaggregated estimates can identify gaps in diagnosing individuals with chronic viral hepatitis. 19. The global target is for ≥90% of people with chronic hepatitis B to be diagnosed. 20. The numerator is the number of people with chronic hepatitis B infection who have been diagnosed with a positive HBsAg test by the end of the reporting year. The denominator is the estimated total number of people with chronic hepatitis B infection (HBsAg positive). 21. Measurement methods include data from program or clinical patient monitoring tools, hepatitis testing records, laboratory registers, antenatal care registers, logbooks, and reporting forms from health facility and community levels. 22. The size of the population infected with chronic hepatitis B should ideally be estimated from nationally representative biomarker surveys. Detailed information on the survey should demonstrate that the study population is representative and that measures were taken to minimize sampling and information bias. 23. Modelling can be used alongside routine program data to estimate the size of the infected population. For example, prevalence data from a population survey conducted at one time may be used to estimate prevalence at a more recent time, considering factors such as treatment coverage, vaccination rates, hepatitis B incidence, and deaths. 24. Disaggregation of data includes age, sex, geographical location, higher-risk populations, pregnancy status, HIV infection status, and HDV coinfection status. 25. The proportion of people with chronic hepatitis C who have been diagnosed is another key indicator. It measures the proportion of individuals with chronic hepatitis C (positive RNA [PCR] or HCV core antigen) who are aware of their infection status. 26. The rationale for this indicator is to estimate the entry point to the continuum of care for people with chronic hepatitis C. Disaggregated estimates can identify gaps in diagnosing individuals with chronic viral hepatitis. 27. The global target is for ≥90% of people with chronic hepatitis C to be diagnosed. 28. The numerator is the number of people with chronic hepatitis C who have been diagnosed with a positive HCV RNA (PCR) or HCV core antigen by the end of the reporting period. The denominator is the estimated total number of people with chronic hepatitis C infection (positive RNA [PCR] or HCV core antigen). 29. Measurement methods include data from program or clinical patient monitoring tools, hepatitis testing records, laboratory registers, logbooks, and reporting forms at the facility and community levels. 30. The size of the population infected with chronic hepatitis C should ideally be estimated from nationally representative biomarker surveys. Detailed information on the survey should demonstrate that the study population is representative and that measures were taken to minimize sampling and information bias. 31. Modelling can be used alongside routine program data to estimate the size of the infected population. For example, prevalence data from a population survey conducted at one time may be used to estimate prevalence at a more recent time, considering factors such as treatment and cure rates, hepatitis C incidence, and deaths. 32. Disaggregation of data includes age, sex, HIV status, geographical location, and higher-risk populations. 33. The proportion of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B initiating treatment among those eligible is a key indicator for treatment and care. It measures progress toward providing treatment to all eligible individuals with chronic hepatitis B. 34. The rationale for this indicator is to monitor the number of people with hepatitis B who were evaluated for disease progression, found eligible for treatment, and placed on antiviral therapy. Disaggregation can indicate equity in enrolling specific priority populations. 35. Trends over time reflect progress in treating people with hepatitis B. This indicator is essential for measuring programmatic targets for the elimination of hepatitis B as a public health threat by 2030. 36. The global target is for ≥80% of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B infection to initiate antiviral therapy. 37. The numerator is the number of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B and eligible for treatment who have initiated antiviral therapy by the end of the reporting period. The denominator is the number of people with chronic hepatitis B infection who have been diagnosed and are eligible for treatment by the end of the reporting period. 38. Measurement methods include program records (clinical records of healthcare facilities providing hepatitis treatment and care). Data on treatment in low-income countries may require extrapolation from select sites until nationwide data becomes available. 39. The proportion of people with chronic hepatitis B currently receiving treatment among those eligible is another key indicator for treatment and care. It measures progress toward providing treatment to all eligible individuals with chronic hepatitis B. 40. The rationale for this indicator is to monitor trends in treating people with hepatitis B and to provide managers with information for forecasting antiviral drug needs and staff allocation to ensure quality care. 41. The numerator is the number of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B and eligible for treatment who are currently receiving antiviral therapy by the end of the reporting period. The denominator is the number of people with chronic hepatitis B infection who have been diagnosed and are eligible for treatment by the end of the reporting period. 42. Retention and attrition analysis should be conducted as part of reporting on this indicator. The numerator should exclude people who have stopped treatment, died, or were otherwise lost to follow-up during the reporting period. These status classification categories should be reported separately at the national level.
